sections.title_en: 1. The Mitzva of "You Shall Not Stand by the Blood of Your Neighbour"
sections.body_en:
It is a great Torah mitzva to save a person who is in danger. For we are commanded even to return to a person an object he has lost, as it is said (Devarim 22:2): "and you shall return it to him"; all the more so must we return his life to him and save him. And likewise the mitzva is learned from the verse (Vayikra 19:16): "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour," as our Sages said (Sanhedrin 73a): From where do we know that one who sees his fellow drowning in a river, or a wild beast dragging him and about to tear him apart, or bandits coming upon him to kill him – from where do we know that he is obligated to save him? Scripture says: "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour."

That is, in addition to the fundamental mitzva "You shall love your neighbour as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), about which Rabbi Akiva said that it is a great principle of the Torah, and which obviously includes within it all the good relations that ought to prevail between a person and his fellow – in addition to this the Torah spelled out a further command, "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour." It is not enough to smile at one's friend, and sometimes even to help him when there is time… rather, the Torah establishes that a person has responsibility and is a guarantor towards his fellow. If his fellow is in trouble, he is obligated to rise to his aid, and not to spare effort or money in saving his friend.

If we indeed conduct ourselves so, and feel in our hearts the mutual responsibility that exists among all Israel, there is no doubt that the society we build here will be more cohesive and united, and will be able to cope with the great challenges from within and without.

sections.title_en: 2. Must the Rescuer Endanger His Own Life?
sections.body_en:
A central question in the mitzva of "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" is how far the obligation of this mitzva extends. It is clear to all that one who sees his fellow in danger – for example, bandits are coming to kill him, or he is drowning in a river – is obligated to rise and save him.

But the question is what the law is in a case where, in order to save his friend, the rescuer must endanger his own life. Is the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" incumbent on him then too, so that he must enter the danger in order to save his fellow, or is the mitzva incumbent on the rescuer only when he does not endanger his own life?

For example, a person passing in the street saw a house going up in flames, and from inside it children were screaming for help. He knows that if he tries to enter the house to save them, it is very possible that he too will choke from the smoke, be burned and die. In such a case must he enter the danger in order to save the children, or perhaps, where there is a real danger, there is no obligation to endanger oneself in order to save the life of another Jew?

Answer: Two main approaches were stated in this halakha. Some say that as a rule the mitzva of "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" is like the other mitzvot of the Torah, and just as there is no mitzva to endanger one's life in order to fulfil other mitzvot, so a person need not endanger his life in order to save his fellow. And some say that the mitzva of "You shall not stand" is different from the other mitzvot, and since his fellow is in danger of death, it is a mitzva to enter a doubtful danger in order to save him.

And since this topic is fundamental, we will expand in the next halakha on the explanation of the two approaches. But we note that the whole discussion of the mitzva of "You shall not stand" concerns an ordinary person in civilian life. In time of war, however, the duty to be prepared to take risks and to fight does not derive from this mitzva, but from the mitzva of war. And if it is required by the order of the senior command, the soldier is obligated to enter real danger, even into a situation in which the greatest likelihood is that he will not return alive from the battle. For in time of war the reckoning is national, and in order to win, individuals must be prepared to endanger their lives (see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 4:1; 4:3).

According to the first approach, which is the view of most poskim, a person is not commanded to enter danger to life in order to save his fellow. For the mitzvot of the Torah were given in order to live by them and not in order that people die through them, as the Sages said: "'And live by them' – and not die by them" (Yoma 85b). And this rule applies also to the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour." If so, the Torah's mitzva to rise to the aid of one's fellow does not oblige a person to endanger his life.

Nevertheless, it is clear that one should not be too afraid of dangers at a time when one's fellow is in danger of death. For just as a person is prepared to take a little risk in order to earn a living, so at the very least he must take a risk in order to save his fellow. After all, there are people who in their work climb to high places, and there are those who sail to distant seas, and there are those who work with dangerous materials. And likewise every person whose property is going up in flames is prepared to take a slight risk in order to save what can be saved; all the more so, in order to save a fellow, it is a mitzva to take a little risk. And so it is explained in the baraita (Sanhedrin 73a) that a person must be prepared to take a little risk in order to save his fellow, such as jumping into a river to save a drowning person, and rising against wild beasts or bandits to save the one attacked. And the Sages said that whoever is excessively careful and fearful will be punished measure for measure, and in the end the same thing will happen to him and people will not come to his aid (Pitḥei Teshuva ḤM 426:2; MB 329:19). But in a situation where saving the fellow requires entering real danger to life, a person is not commanded to save his fellow. For according to this view, the rule "and live by them" applies also to the mitzva of saving a fellow. Real danger to life is defined as a danger that an ordinary person is not prepared to take even in order to save all his property.

To sum up: any action that involves a real risk to life, which an ordinary person is not prepared to enter even in order to save his property – there is no mitzva to take that risk in order to save one's fellow. And this is the view of most poskim.[1]

But according to the second approach, the mitzva of "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" is different from the other mitzvot, because it deals with saving human life. Therefore it obliges us to enter a real danger to life in order to save one's fellow from certain death. And even if it is a danger that an ordinary person is not prepared to take upon himself in order to save his property, nevertheless, in order to save another person, one must enter even a real danger. All this is on condition that, although the rescue operation is dangerous and there is a risk that both will die, nevertheless according to the greater likelihood the rescue operation will succeed and both will live. But if the situation is that the rescue operation is so dangerous that there is only a fifty percent chance that it will succeed, and on the other hand fifty percent that it will fail and both will die, in such a case one should not enter a doubtful danger in order to save.

The reason for this is that in principle his life and his fellow's life are equal, but of course every person must first look after himself. However, when his fellow is in certain danger, and in order to save him he must enter a situation of doubtful danger, where most of the chances lean towards success, it is preferable to take into account the certain danger of his fellow and the great chances of rescue, rather than to fear his own doubtful danger. For through the rescue operation the greatest likelihood is that both will live. But in a situation where the chances of rescue and of failure are equal, every person must first look after himself.[2]

In practice, the halakha was ruled that by strict law a person need not put himself into danger beyond what ordinary people risk for the sake of their property and their livelihood. But it is a trait of piety to take a risk for the sake of saving one's fellow even beyond that, as long as it is clear that the greater likelihood is that the rescue operation will succeed.[3]

notes_en.en:
So ruled Rabbeinu Yona Gerondi in Sefer Issur Ve-Heter, kelal 59, din 38, that a person should not enter a doubtful danger in order to save his fellow from certain danger. And so ruled the Sma ḤM 426:2, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav OḤ 329:8, and Laws of Damage to Body and Soul 7; MB 329:19. And so ruled Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 174:2, and Responsa Tzitz Eliezer part 9, 45, and others.
The reasoning that a person must take a little risk in order to save his fellow, just as he takes a risk to save his property, is based on the baraita in Sanhedrin 73a, and so it is brought in the Rambam and SA ḤM 426. And so Rabbi Unterman expanded and explained in "Tzomet Ha-Torah Ve-Ha-Medina", part 3, p. 319; and see the article of Rabbi Zilberstein in Assia part 7, p. 4.

This is the view of the Beit Yosef ḤM 426, based on the author of Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of the Yerushalmi. Regarding the view of the Radbaz, who expanded on the explanation of this topic in two important responsa, there is a dispute among the poskim. From what he wrote in part 5, siman 1582 (218), it appears that his view is that a person is commanded to enter danger in order to save his fellow, provided that most of the chances are that the rescue will succeed, as the second approach. But some learned from the responsum in part 3, 627 that his view is like the first approach, for there he ruled that a person is not obligated to agree that his hand be cut off in order to save his fellow. And one can say that cutting off a hand is worse in a person's eyes than a doubtful danger in which the greater chances are of success, and as the Shakh wrote (YD 157:3), that the loss of a limb is equivalent to self-sacrifice. See Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:84, Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 174:4, Tzitz Eliezer part 9, 45, Minḥat Yitzḥak part 6, 103. And Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Kook, in La-Netivot Yisrael part 1, p. 119, proves from the Talmud and the Rambam that a person is obligated to take a real risk in order to save his fellow, and the condition is that he is able to save him.
Because of the importance of the matter, one should know that at first sight it seems from the words of the great posek Rabbi Yosef Karo that he has a third view, according to which even if the chances are equal – fifty percent that he will succeed in his task and save his fellow, and fifty percent that he will fail and he too will die – he is obligated to take the risk in order to try to save him. But in practice most poskim disagree with him, and as we will see, it is reasonable that even in his view this is not the halakha. Let us clarify this a little:
The basis of the words of Rabbi Yosef Karo is the Jerusalem Talmud, Terumot end of chapter 8, where it is related that Rav Assi (some read Rabbi Ammi) was seized by bandits who were about to kill him. Rabbi Yonatan said: Let the dead man be wrapped in his shrouds (that is, he despaired of trying to save his life). Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: I will go and try to save him; either I will succeed in killing the bandits, or they will kill me. He went, and in the end succeeded in persuading them to release Rabbi Assi. From here the great posek Rabbi Yosef Karo learned that a person is commanded to enter a doubtful danger in order to save his fellow from certain danger. And some wanted to learn from this that in his view, even if there are equal chances – fifty percent that he will succeed in his task and come out safely, and fifty percent that he himself too will be killed – nevertheless it is a mitzva to save, because he enters only a doubtful danger while his fellow is in certain danger. And as Reish Lakish did, who entered a situation where either he would kill or be killed.
But first one must question whether this is indeed the view of the Yerushalmi, for it is possible to say that Reish Lakish himself knew that there was a sixty percent chance he would succeed in saving him, but since there was also about forty percent that he would fail and be killed, he said, either I will save or I will be killed. And it is known that Reish Lakish knew how to deal with bandits, as explained in Gittin 47b and Bava Metzia 84a. In addition, there is no proof that the halakha follows Reish Lakish; perhaps the law follows Rabbi Yonatan, who held that in such a situation one should not try to save, and said "Let the dead man be wrapped in his shrouds." And further, from the Bavli, Sanhedrin 73a, it is proven that one should not enter such a doubtful danger, as explained in the book Agudat Ezov brought in the Pitḥei Teshuva ḤM 426:2, and so wrote Responsa Yad Eliyahu 43. And on this basis all the other poskim ruled that one should not enter so great a doubt of danger. If so, so as not to multiply disputes, it is preferable to explain the Yerushalmi in a way that does not disagree with the Babylonian Talmud.
In addition, the Netziv, in Ha'amek She'ala 129:4, explained that even according to the Yerushalmi there is no obligation to enter a fifty percent doubt of danger, but that in the view of the Yerushalmi this is a custom of piety. And in Responsa Yad Eliyahu he wrote that even according to the Yerushalmi one should not enter a doubtful danger to save a fellow, and there Reish Lakish entered a doubtful danger to save Rav Assi because he held that Rav Assi was greater than he in Torah, and therefore he wanted to endanger himself to save him. But in an ordinary case, even according to the Yerushalmi it is forbidden to enter a fifty percent doubt of danger to save a fellow. And even when it is a matter of saving a great Torah scholar, it is not an obligation but only a custom of piety; the proof is that Rabbi Yonatan said "Let the dead man be wrapped in his shrouds." It turns out, then, that it is not at all clear that the Yerushalmi indeed holds that one must enter an evenly balanced doubt of danger to life, and also by reasoning such a thing should not be obligatory; and even the Beit Yosef said only to enter a doubt of life, and it is reasonable that even forty percent danger is called a doubt of life, and it is reasonable that this is what he meant, and not a danger of fifty percent.
In addition, if his intention had been to rule that a person must enter a fifty percent risk in order to save his fellow, why did he not write so in his important book the Shulḥan Arukh? Therefore it is right that we say that in the view of Rabbi Yosef Karo one must enter a doubt of life in order to save a fellow, but all this on condition that most of the chances lean towards rescue. And therefore we have two views and not three.

This is the view of most poskim, among them: Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 174:4; Rabbi Yisraeli, Shevilin 5737; Sha'arei Ezra ḤM 125; Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:84; see Ha-Tzava Ke-Hilkhata 14:4. And further see Tiferet Yisrael Yoma 8:3. The Netziv in Ha'amek She'ala 129:4 wrote that it is permitted even to enter a doubtful danger in order to save a fellow. And so it appears from Mishpat Kohen 143. But from Tzitz Eliezer 9:45 it is implied that it is forbidden. But as stated, most poskim hold that it is a custom of piety.

sections.body_en:
We have learned that a person is not obligated to enter real danger in order to save his fellow, but that there is a mitzva and a trait of piety in this. On this basis the law regarding organ donation from a living person is understood: there is no obligation to donate, but there is a trait of piety in it. For example, there is no obligation to donate one lobe of the lungs for someone suffering from cystic fibrosis. And likewise there is no obligation to donate part of the liver for someone suffering from cirrhosis of the liver, whose life is in danger. And likewise regarding a kidney. For there is no obligation to save one's fellow while taking a real risk oneself. But one who volunteers and donates fulfils a great mitzva, and there is a trait of piety in this.

Admittedly, it is possible that in some of these donations there is no real danger, and nevertheless there is no obligation to donate. For the Radbaz wrote that there is no obligation to donate a limb in order to save one's fellow (and see below 14:1-2).

Regarding blood donation, it is clear that there is a mitzva to donate blood for a fellow who is in danger. But the question is whether according to the Torah a person can be obliged to donate of his blood. Rabbi Wosner wrote that in a situation where there is a dangerously ill person who needs a rare blood type, one who has that blood type is obligated to donate in order to save him. And even a person who fears that he may become slightly ill as a result of the donation is obligated to donate, since there is no danger in donating blood, and slight distress or the fear of a mild illness cannot serve as an excuse for evading the fulfilment of the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" (Shevet Ha-Levi 5:219).

Admittedly, at a time when there are other people who can donate blood, it is reasonable that a weak person may say, it is preferable that people healthier and stronger than I donate. But when there is no one to donate, and a person's life is in danger, one is obligated to donate blood (see Responsa Tzitz Eliezer 16:23).

Rabbi Feinstein was asked whether a person may donate blood in exchange for monetary payment. The reason for the question is that a person is forbidden to wound himself; the question, then, is whether a person may wound himself for money. Rabbi Feinstein answered that it is permitted, because this is not considered wounding, for in times past people were accustomed to let blood as a remedy. And although today this is not considered a remedy, nevertheless we will not consider blood donation as forbidden wounding (Igrot Moshe ḤM 1:103). And further, the whole prohibition of wounding oneself applies specifically in a way of disgrace and damage, but here, for medical benefit and monetary profit, there is no prohibition. In addition, Rabbi Auerbach said that since there is a mitzva of saving lives in blood donation, it is not called wounding (Nishmat Avraham YD 349, p. 265). And some wrote that ideally it is preferable to donate blood not in order to receive payment (Responsa Va-Yeshev Moshe part 1, 93-94).

sections.title_en: 5. Must a Doctor Take a Risk in Order to Save a Patient?
sections.body_en:
Question: A doctor who was summoned to treat a patient with a dangerous and contagious disease – must he treat the patient at a risk to himself, or may he evade the treatment on the grounds that it is his duty to take care of his health and his life?

Answer: The doctor's duty is to treat patients even if they are ill with a contagious disease. The reason for this is that we have already learned that the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" obliges a person to save his fellow from danger. And when the rescue requires the rescuer to put himself into real danger, according to halakha there is no obligation to take the risk, but it is a trait of piety to take the risk in order to save. If so, a doctor who earns his living from his work, and has taken upon himself everything that is accepted in the world of medicine, cannot claim: I do not want to treat a contagious disease. For by the very fact that he accepted the role of doctor he undertook to conduct himself with a trait of piety that includes taking a certain risk for the sake of saving the lives of patients.

And further, even for the sake of a livelihood a person is permitted to endanger himself a little, and to work in jobs that require dangerous voyages or climbing poles and high places, or working with dangerous materials. All the more so is a doctor permitted to take a risk in his livelihood in order to save human life. And if he undertook this when he entered the role, it is his duty to keep his promise.

And likewise it is clear that hospitals must oblige the doctors to treat patients with contagious diseases, for it is not possible, from a public point of view, that those patients be abandoned to their fate until their souls depart. Therefore doctors were hired, so that they would treat the patients, and one who, after taking all the accepted precautions, does not want to treat them must resign from his post as a doctor.

And it is related of great sages of Israel, among them Rabbi Yisrael of Salant, that when the cholera epidemic broke out he organised a group at whose head he stood, and he and the members of the group treated all the sick. And many times, in the merit of the mitzva, specifically those who treated the sick were saved from the epidemic. The reason for this is that it is not possible that dangerously ill people be abandoned to their fate.

Admittedly, the poskim disagreed as to whether there is a mitzva to visit someone who is ill with a disease when there is a reasonable risk that the visitor will be infected by his illness. In the view of the author of the Knesset Ha-Gedola it is a mitzva to visit, whereas in the view of the author of the Shulḥan Gavoha it is forbidden to visit. But it is clear that the public as a whole is obligated to see to it that someone treats the patient. And doctors and nurses are designated for this role, and therefore they are not permitted to say that by reason of the mitzva of guarding one's life they do not want to treat these patients.

The doctor must also treat AIDS patients: first, because he undertook this, and second, if he is careful not to touch his blood the risk of infection is negligible. And even one who must operate on him can take precautions and reduce the risk to such a low level that it need not be taken into account. And one cannot argue that perhaps this patient is to blame for his illness because he sinned with homosexual intercourse. First, because it is possible that he became ill for another reason; second, even if he sinned, perhaps his law in this matter is that of one acting unintentionally and under compulsion, since he did not know the severity of the transgression (see the article of Rabbi Prof. Steinberg, Assia 7, p. 79).

However, a doctor in the early stages of pregnancy who is called to treat a patient with rubella is exempt from treating him. For if she is infected with rubella there is a twenty percent chance that she will miscarry or that the child will be born with a defect. And since there are other doctors, there is no reason that she specifically should treat the rubella patient. And further, even when she took upon herself to be a doctor, in all likelihood she did not undertake to enter a special risk relating to the period of pregnancy (see Tzitz Eliezer 9:17:5; and the article of Rabbi Zilberstein, Assia 7, pp. 3-7).

sections.title_en: 6. The Mitzva to Save by Means of Money
sections.body_en:
We have learned that a person is commanded to save his fellow from danger, and even to take a certain risk for his sake. Therefore a person who sees his fellow drowning in a river, and he knows how to swim and estimates that he is able to save him from drowning, must jump in and save him. And likewise a person who sees criminals rising against his fellow to kill him, and he estimates that he has the strength to stand against them and save him, is commanded to do so.

And our Sages added in tractate Sanhedrin (73a) a further detail in this law: that this mitzva does not include only physical effort for the fellow, such as pulling him out of the river or shielding him with one's body from his attackers, but the mitzva also includes the effort of money. If it is possible to save the fellow by means of money or property, one is obligated to do so.

For example, a person whose fellow is very ill and needs medical treatment in order to be saved – everyone who is able is commanded to come to his aid. And likewise the doctor is obligated to treat a poor patient who is unable to pay for the treatment. And about doctors who are not prepared to treat poor patients, our Sages said: "The best of doctors – to Gehinnom" (Kiddushin 82a).

I heard of a case that provides a further example of this halakha. A bus was hit by a firebomb, and the fire caught one person, and in order to save him from the fire and prevent the burns from deepening it was necessary to take a blanket or a coat to smother the fire. Regrettably, a non-combat soldier standing beside the injured person spared his coat and refused to give it for the wounded man, and so precious seconds passed until another person took off his coat and helped smother the fire. According to halakha, of course that soldier was obligated to give his coat to the wounded man, as it is said: "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour."

From a national point of view too, when we see a certain community attacked and threatened by terror and attacks, whether it is in Judea, Samaria and Gaza or beside another border, the whole public in the country must feel full responsibility for the welfare of the residents of that area, and do everything in order to remove the threat from them. And if it appears that the government is negligent in its role, it is a mitzva to protest against it until the situation changes for the better.

sections.title_en: 7. Must One Give All One's Money to Save a Life?
sections.body_en:
A central question in the laws of saving lives that is important to clarify is how far a person is required to give of his money for the sake of saving his fellow. For example, a person who knows that his fellow needs a very expensive operation, which costs several hundred thousand shekels, and he has no way of paying for it. Must he sell his house and all his property and give all his money in order to save his fellow, or is there a limit to how much a person must give of his property in order to save his fellow?[4]

In general it can be learned from the words of the author of the Ḥafetz Ḥayim in his book Ahavat Ḥesed (part 2, 20:2) that although in general a person is forbidden to give more than a fifth of all his money to tzedaka, lest he become poor in the end and need the help of others, nevertheless, if his fellow is in danger to life, the measure of a fifth does not apply, and it is a mitzva to give more than a fifth for the sake of saving him. And from this one can infer that it is only a mitzva to give more than a fifth, but not an obligation (so Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach inferred, as brought in Nishmat Adam ḤM 426:1).

And likewise it is reasonable that the Torah cannot command a person to give all the money and property that he accumulated throughout his life. In all likelihood he had plans for using the money; perhaps he planned to marry off his children, or to keep money for his old age. And if in one day he had to give all his property for the sake of saving another person, his mind and the minds of his family might become unhinged. And mental derangement is considered danger to life.[5]

Rabbi Shmuel Ha-Levi Wosner shlita made a great new point in this law: when it is a matter of a patient who lives in a community, the obligation to save him rests on the whole community, and not on the individual. Therefore the individual is not commanded to sell all his property in order to save the patient. Admittedly, if the patient and he were in an isolated place, and a situation arose in which only if he sold all his property could he save his fellow from death, he would indeed be commanded to do so. But as long as they are part of a community, there is no obligation on the individual to save his fellow by himself (Shevet Ha-Levi part 5, 174; and see the book Nishmat Adam ḤM 426:1, which mentioned a difficulty raised by Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach ztz"l against this).

At the same time, of course, everyone who knows the dangerously ill person must give as much as he can to save him. And as is known, every person must set aside a tenth of his money for tzedaka. And some say that in such a situation of danger, everyone is obligated to give a fifth of his money to tzedaka (see Ahavat Ḥesed part 2, 19:4).

notes_en.en:
One should know that as a rule a person is obligated to spend up to a tenth of his money in order to fulfil a positive mitzva, and at most up to a fifth. But in order not to transgress a negative commandment, he should give all his money, as explained in the Rema OḤ 656. And seemingly, according to this, he must give all his money in order not to transgress "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour." But "You shall not stand" is a negative commandment that involves no action, and there is a dispute about this. In the view of the Rivash 387, even in order not to transgress a negative commandment that involves no action one must give all one's property, whereas according to the Ḥavvot Ya'ir 139 the law of a negative commandment that involves no action is like the law of a positive mitzva, that a person may spend up to a fifth and no more. But in halakha the view of most poskim is like the Rivash, as written in the Sedei Ḥemed, ma'arekhet lamed, siman 107.
It is fitting to add here that in the Responsa Ḥatam Sofer ḤM end of siman 177 he explained how there can be a reasoning that one does not redeem captives for more than their value so as not to cause hardship to the public; for seemingly, for the sake of saving lives one should give everything. And he answered that at a time when wicked nations rule over Israel, hardship for the public too is considered a matter of danger to life. For many times we have had to buy our lives with money, and if the public becomes impoverished, it is possible that a decree will come upon Israel and the community will not have the money to annul it. And the Shevet Ha-Levi wrote that today, thank God, there is no such concern, and this reasoning should not be used.
In my humble opinion, this reasoning can still be used regarding the general economic situation: that it is not possible to impose excessively high taxes even for the sake of saving lives in hospitals. For if the economy as a whole is harmed, in the end the state will not have the money to continue developing education, research, the economy and industry, and our dependence on the nations of the world will increase, and we will not be able to cope properly with security problems; and the matter requires further study.

Similarly the Radbaz wrote (part 3, 627, and in the Ḥadashot 1052) that if a cruel ruler said to a Jew, either let me cut off your hand or I will kill your fellow, despite the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour," and although cutting off the hand would not cause his death, the Jew is not obligated to agree that his hand be cut off in order to save his fellow. And he brings several reasonings there, and finally says: And further, it is written, "Its ways are ways of pleasantness," and the laws of the Torah must accord with reason and logic; and how could it occur to us that a person should allow his eyes to be blinded or his hand or foot cut off so that they will not kill his fellow? Therefore this is a trait of piety, to donate one of one's limbs for one's fellow, but there is no obligation in it.

sections.title_en: 8. The Mitzva to Save One's Fellow's Money
sections.body_en:
The mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour," whose main concern is to come to the aid of a fellow who is in danger, includes within it, according to our Sages, also a mitzva to come to the aid of one's fellow when his money or property is in danger. For example, a person who has testimony that can benefit his fellow is obligated to come and testify before a beit din in order to save his fellow's money. For example, a person who saw Reuven lend money to Shimon, and afterwards heard that Shimon denies the loan and refuses to repay it – he and everyone who saw the loan are obligated to come and testify about it before the beit din, in order to save Reuven's money so that it is not lost.

And likewise one who sees a thief going to steal property or money from his fellow is obligated to act with all his ability to foil the theft. Obviously there is no mitzva here to give up one's life in order to save one's fellow's money, and therefore one should not stand with bare hands against robbers drawing pistols. But at the same time one must not be too afraid, and one should do what is possible to prevent the theft. And a person who has the strength to stop the thief by himself is commanded to do so. And if he cannot, he is commanded to try to shout "Thief!" with all his strength, in order to summon more people and to deter the thief and drive him off.

To sum up, the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" exists not only because of the immense value of human life, but it also expresses the mutual guarantee and responsibility that ought to exist between each one of Israel towards his fellow. Obviously the value of life cannot be compared to the value of money, and therefore the devotion required for the sake of saving human life is incomparably greater than the devotion for saving money. But from the aspect of mutual responsibility, we also have responsibility towards the money of others, and we are commanded to act in order to save it.

sections.title_en: 9. Is One Who Does Not Save Punished According to the Torah?
sections.body_en:
Question: A person who could have saved his fellow or his money, and was negligent and refused to save him – according to the Torah must he be punished or not?

Answer: As is known, the mitzvot of the Torah are divided in two: positive mitzvot and negative mitzvot. In general the Torah did not set a punishment for one who neglects a positive mitzva; the punishment is the loss of the mitzva. But for one who transgressed a negative mitzva the Torah set a punishment. For severe transgressions such as murder or idolatry the Torah set the death penalty [in practice, for halakhic reasons, only rarely, less than once in seven years, did the beit din sentence a person to death; but in principle this is the punishment for severe transgressions]. And for light transgressions such as eating forbidden foods the Torah set the punishment of lashes.

But although the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" is a negative mitzva, and seemingly one who could have saved his fellow and did not do so should have been punished by the beit din with lashes, nevertheless, because this transgression is committed without an action, one does not receive lashes for it. This is the rule: for a transgression committed by an action the Torah set a punishment, such as a person who ate pork or desecrated Shabbat. But one who transgressed by being idle and not acting – the matter is like the neglect of a positive mitzva, for which there is no punishment in this world; only in the World of Truth, the world of souls, will he be punished and his standing harmed. And so is the law regarding one who saw his fellow drowning and did not jump in to save him: the Torah did not set a punishment for him in this world.

The Rambam wrote about this (Laws of the Murderer 1:16): Although one does not receive lashes for these negative commandments, because there is no action in them, nevertheless they are severe, for whoever destroys one soul of Israel, it is as though he destroyed the whole world entire; and whoever sustains one soul of Israel, it is as though he sustained the whole world entire.

One should learn from this halakha how great is the duty on each one of us to act with all his strength, whether by protests or by explanation, against failures in security policy. By their very nature these failures claim victims, whether in the north of the country or in its centre. And whoever is negligent in protesting against this transgresses "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour."

sections.title_en: 10. Saving Life Overrides the Fulfilment of Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
It is a great mitzva to guard life and sustain it. And so great is this mitzva that the Sages said that it overrides all the mitzvot of the Torah, as it is said (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My ordinances, which if a person does them he shall live by them; I am the Lord." And the Sages learned from here that all the mitzvot were given so that people would live by them, and not so that they would die through them; and therefore saving life overrides all the mitzvot (Yoma 85b).

The purpose of all the mitzvot is to increase life and blessing in the world, for through the mitzvot a person connects to the Creator of the world, the source of all life. Therefore when life itself is in danger, the first aim is to guard it.

For example: a dangerously ill person who, in order to save his life, must be fed forbidden foods must eat them in order to be saved. And likewise an ill person for whom the Yom Kippur fast is dangerous is commanded to eat and drink on Yom Kippur (SA OḤ 618:1). And likewise regarding brit mila: in a situation where the baby is ill and there is a concern that the brit will endanger his life, although by law one must circumcise specifically on the eighth day, it is forbidden to circumcise him as long as he is ill, because saving life overrides all the mitzvot (SA YD 263:1).

The best-known mitzva that is many times overridden for the sake of saving life is the mitzva of Shabbat. And although the value of Shabbat is known, and the Sages said of it that it is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, nevertheless, whenever there is before us a sick person whose life is in danger, it is a mitzva to desecrate Shabbat for him in order to save him.

And even when a person is in a situation of doubtful danger to life, it is a mitzva to hurry and desecrate Shabbat in order to save him. And whoever asks a sage at that time whether it is permitted to save a person who is in doubtful danger to life is like one who sheds blood, because by the time he asks the patient may die (SA OḤ 328:2). And even the rabbi who is asked about it is disgraced, because he should have explained in his lessons this fundamental principle that saving life overrides Shabbat, and not caused a situation in which a person lies in danger, and instead of saving him people come and ask whether it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat for him (MB 328:6, in the name of the Yerushalmi).

Therefore the Sages said that where it is necessary to desecrate Shabbat in order to save a sick person, one tries to desecrate Shabbat through the greatest person present in that place, and not through minors or simple people. This is so that all will understand that there is no disregard here, Heaven forbid, for the sanctity of Shabbat, but rather that this is the halakha – that saving life overrides Shabbat – and therefore even the great sages of Israel hurry to desecrate Shabbat in order to save the sick person (SA OḤ 328:12; MB 34).[6]

notes_en.en: Doctors today are accustomed to desecrate Shabbat with labours forbidden by Torah law in order to save a gentile. This is according to the view of Responsa Divrei Ḥayim part 2, 25, and his reason is that if they do not treat gentiles, there is a concern of danger to many Jews: the matter will become known and hatred will increase, and there is a danger that gentiles will not save Jews, and perhaps will even harm them. And so wrote Shemirat Shabbat Ke-hilkhata chapter 40, note 41, in the name of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach. And see Melumdei Milḥama siman 43, which is lenient for one who is considered a ger toshav.

sections.body_en:
We hold a rule: saving life overrides the mitzvot of the Torah. And if wicked people come and force a person to desecrate Shabbat for them, and otherwise they will kill him, he must desecrate Shabbat in order to save his life.

However, three mitzvot are excepted from this rule, in which under no circumstances whatsoever should one listen to the wicked, and about them it was said, "Let him be killed rather than transgress." They are: idolatry, bloodshed and forbidden relations. For these are such severe transgressions that there is no value at all to a life in which one is forced to commit such terrible transgressions.

And one must further know: what we said, that for all the other mitzvot a person must transgress the mitzvot and guard his life – all this is on condition that those wicked people force him to commit transgressions for their own benefit, for example, they want him to work for them on Shabbat. But if all their coercion is aimed at disgracing the Torah, and showing that here is a Jew transgressing the mitzvot of his Torah, then if they forced him to transgress them in private, he should transgress and not be killed; but if they forced him to transgress them in public, that is, ten Jews know of it, he must be killed rather than transgress. For in such a situation it is no longer a matter only of these particular mitzvot, but of the honour of the whole Torah. And for such a principle we are commanded to be killed rather than transgress. And at the time of a royal decree whose aim is to make Israel abandon their religion, then even for a Jewish custom, such as their custom in tying their shoes, one must be killed rather than transgress, because every detail of the decree is in essence aimed against the Torah and the faith of Israel (SA YD 157:1).

Despite the immense importance of life in this world, there are principles and values whose root is in the World of Truth and eternity, and they override all the life of this world. One must know that in the merit of the connection of the people of Israel to those absolute values, the people of Israel lives and endures, and all the wicked of the world have not succeeded and will not succeed in destroying it. Through self-sacrifice and attachment to eternal values, our life is raised to an eternal height, and in this merit we are connected to the World of Truth and merit to inherit the World to Come. Therefore every Jew must know that at a time when he is required to give up his fundamental principles, he must give up his life and not compromise.

There is a further mitzva that overrides the saving of individual lives – the mitzva of conquering the Land. For from the fact that the Torah commanded us to conquer the Land, it is implied that we must fight, and it is clear that the Torah did not command us to rely on a miracle. Therefore the mitzva of conquering the Land and defending it obliges us to be prepared for self-sacrifice (see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 3:4; 4:2).

In the Talmud (Bava Metzia 62a) a fundamental question in the laws of saving life is explained. Two people were walking on a parched road, and in the hand of one of them was a flask of water. If both drink of the water, both will die, because there is still a long way before them. And if one drinks, he will be able to reach a settled place and be saved. What must the owner of the water do – is it his duty to let his fellow drink of the water, share and share alike, or not?

Ben Petura at first expounded: It is better that both drink and die, and that one should not see the death of his fellow. Until Rabbi Akiva came and taught: It is said (Vayikra 25:36), "that your brother may live with you" – your life comes before the life of your fellow. That is, upon every person there rests a mitzva to keep his brother alive with him, but when his own life is in danger, he must first save himself, and only afterwards save his fellow.

And to sharpen the halakha, one should explain that even if the fellow argues, "Give me a little of the water so that I do not die at once, and we will both live a while longer, and perhaps in the meantime other people will find us and save us" – even so, if the likelihood of this is low, and the greatest chances are that in the end both will die, the owner of the water must drink it himself and live. For his life comes before the life of his fellow (Ha'amek She'ala 147). For we have learned that a person need not save his fellow while taking such a risk that by the greater chances he will die.

And so is the halakha in similar cases: two people drowning in the sea, and one found a life ring that can keep only him afloat – he need not give it to his fellow. And likewise two sick people who need a rare medicine that has run out, and one of them is rich and able to buy it for himself – if the quantity suffices for him alone, he need not share it with his sick fellow.

But it still remains to clarify whether a person may of his own will sacrifice his life for the sake of saving his fellow, that is, give up the water in his hand and give it to his fellow. In the view of several poskim it is forbidden: since the water is in his hands and he has the power to go on living, it is his duty to guard his own life first. Moreover, from the fact that the water is in his hand, it is a sign that Heaven wants him to live, and if he gives the water to his fellow it is like suicide (Rabbi Unterman, see "Be-Tzomet Ha-Torah Ve-Ha-Medina" part 3, p. 315; Rabbi Feinstein, Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 174:4).

But in the view of a good number of poskim, since in principle his life and his fellow's life are equal, he is permitted to give himself up for his fellow. And this is not considered suicide, since there is no harm to life here, for there is no difference whether in the end he lives or his fellow (the Netziv, She'iltot 147; the author of the Or Ha-Ḥayim in his book Rishon Le-Tziyon YD 247:1; Rav Kook in Mishpat Kohen 143). And if it is a matter of saving a Torah scholar, the author of Sefer Ḥasidim (siman 698), who was one of the great Rishonim in Ashkenaz, wrote that it is fitting to give up one's life for the sake of saving a Torah scholar whom the public needs (further see the article of Rabbi Bar-Ilan, Assia part 7, p. 181).

On the redemption of captives, see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land", chapter 7, halakhot 6-8. And on whether one must save a terrorist whom people want to kill, see there 7:7.

A rodef is one who is about to kill his fellow. In such a case, according to halakha, the one attacked is commanded to stand and defend himself in order to save his life. This defence includes attack as well; that is, if in order to save himself he is forced to strike first and kill the attacker, he is permitted to do so, as our Sages said: "If someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first" (Sanhedrin 72a).

Not only must the one attacked defend himself, but every person who sees the rodef about to kill his fellow is obligated to do everything to prevent him from killing. If there is time, he should first turn to the rodef and warn him not to harm his fellow. If even so he did not listen to his words, or there is no time to speak with him, everyone is commanded to strike the rodef and prevent him from carrying out his plot. Of course, if it is possible to prevent the murder by wounding the rodef, one should wound him and not kill him. But when the event happens quickly, and there is a concern that by the time the rescuer tries to aim precisely and strike one of the rodef's limbs, the murderer will manage to carry out his plot – the rescuer is commanded to do everything to save the one pursued, even by an action that may kill the rodef. Afterwards, one cannot argue against the rescuer, "Why did you not content yourself with wounding him?" For in such situations the main thing is to react quickly, and it is hard to weigh precisely the degree of force that should be used. Therefore, as long as the rescuer acted in good faith, and did not intend to take revenge on the rodef, but his aim was to save the one pursued – he is not to be blamed if he killed the rodef (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer, chapter 1, halakhot 6-7, 13-14).

And although regarding all the transgressions of the Torah we have a clear rule that one does not punish a person before he has committed the sin, and even after he has sinned, only the beit din has the authority to punish him – nevertheless, in the matter of a rodef the law is the reverse. For here the aim is to save the one pursued, and therefore specifically before the murder has been carried out it is permitted to strike the rodef in order to prevent the murder; whereas after the murder it is forbidden to harm him, and he must be brought to trial.

Every person who is able to save the one attacked, and refrained and did not kill the rodef, has neglected a positive mitzva, as it is said (Devarim 25:12): "you shall cut off her hand," and has transgressed two negative mitzvot: "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" (Vayikra 19:16), and "your eye shall not pity" (Devarim 25:12). And although one who is negligent and does not save is not punished for it, nevertheless he has a severe transgression on his hands, for whoever sustains one soul of Israel, it is as though he sustained the whole world entire (Rambam there 1:15-16).

According to halakha, the law is the same also regarding a married woman: if a man pursues her in order to rape her, it is a mitzva to save her. Ideally, of course, one should not harm the life of the one pursuing to rape. But when the only way to save her is by harming the life of the one coming to rape, it is permitted to kill him (Rambam there 1:10-12).

The law of the moser existed when Jews lived under the tyrannical rule of gentiles, and one Jew could endanger the lives of many of Israel. A "moser" is a Jew who informs on his fellow Jews before the gentiles, and causes the gentiles to come and kill Jews, or even only take their money. And one warns him and says to him: "Do not inform." And if he is brazen and says, "I will not listen to you, but I will go and inform," it is a mitzva to kill him, and whoever kills him first has merited (Rambam, Laws of Wounding and Damaging 8:10; SA ḤM 388:10). And all the more so one who helps the gentiles with his own hands to take lives or money from Israel is a "moser".

The moser is not killed as a punishment for his evil deed; the fact is that if he has already informed and handed over his fellow to the gentiles, there is no permission to kill him. Rather, the whole reason for which it is a mitzva to kill the moser is in order to save the one informed on from the danger that the moser is about to bring upon him. For just as it is a mitzva to kill a person who pursues his fellow to kill him with his own hands, so it is a mitzva to kill a person who is preparing to hand over his fellow to the gentiles, since in both cases there is a rodef who endangers his fellow's life. Therefore every person is commanded to save the one pursued from the rodef. And since there is no other way to prevent the informing, there is no choice: it is a mitzva to save the one pursued by killing the moser.

And even if that person threatens to hand over a small amount of money to the gentiles, even in such a case it is a mitzva to kill him. For example, the gentiles are searching for straw and hay to confiscate for their needs, and the moser is preparing to inform before them that a certain Jew is hiding a storehouse of straw and hay – even then it is permitted to kill him. For the long and bitter experience of thousands of years of antisemitism has proven that when a Jew's money is handed over to the gentiles, that Jew may in the end be killed by them. Therefore the handing over of money too is considered the handing over of lives, and so every Jew bears a mitzva to save the one pursued (Responsa Rivash 238, based on Bava Kamma 117a and Berakhot 58a).

We have already mentioned that if the moser has already carried out his plot, one may not kill him. The reason for this is that here it is no longer a matter of preventing the danger, but of punishment and revenge, and this is permitted only by decision of the beit din or the leaders of the community. But if that person is known to inform, and there is a reasonable concern that he will continue to hand over his fellow Jews to the gentiles, then even after he has carried out his plot it is a mitzva to kill him, so that he will not continue to hand over others (Rambam there, halakha 11, and SA ḤM 388:13).

To prevent error, it is important to note here that the law of the moser applies to an individual who acts on his own initiative and causes danger to life for another Jew. But public figures who think they are acting for the good of their people, and by mistake cause risk to their fellows, are not considered mosrim. They may be considered mistaken, and if it becomes clear that their mistake is grave, the public can bring them to trial for it; but it is clear that their law is not the law of a "moser", and private individuals are forbidden to harm them.
